content.title: About
content.content: Asparagus is the young shoot of the herbaceous plant Asparagus officinalis, cultivated in temperate regions. Fresh asparagus has a delicate, slightly nutty flavor and a crisp texture. Cooking it with a small amount of oil enhances its aroma and makes its nutrients more bioavailable.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Asparagus is one of the oldest cultivated vegetables, grown for over 2,000 years.
In ancient Rome, asparagus was considered a delicacy reserved for the elite.
There are three main varieties: green, white (grown in darkness), and purple.
The harvest season in the Northern Hemisphere typically runs from April to June.
Light sautéing in oil brings out aromatic compounds that are otherwise muted.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Asparagus provides folate (B9), vitamin B6, and thiamine, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Low‑calorie fiber source
items.content: One cup of cooked asparagus delivers about 2 g of dietary fiber, aiding digestion and satiety.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: It contains glutathione, vitamin C, and vitamin E, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Heart‑supporting nutrients
items.content: Potassium and folate help maintain normal blood pressure, while plant compounds may improve lipid profiles.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: Asparagus supplies iron, magnesium, and zinc, essential for blood formation and immune health.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to asparagus, such as skin rash or swelling.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Asparagus contains oxalates, which in excess can contribute to kidney stone formation.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: For sensitive people, large portions may cause gas and abdominal discomfort.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Quickly sauté asparagus in olive or sunflower oil, add it to salads, soups, or pasta. Before cooking, trim the tough outer part of the stalk. Lightly browned asparagus retains its crunch and aroma while improving absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh asparagus in the refrigerator wrapped in a slightly damp towel and placed in a plastic bag; use within 3–5 days. Cooked asparagus should be kept in an airtight container in the fridge and consumed within 2 days.
